## The founder-emulation items

1. **Who (practitioner `agent`).** YC-C names hotel groups with "call centers and central reservation departments";
   YC-L's video features front-desk staff at a Munich hotel. *My choice:* the reservation agent, central office or
   front desk, who sees the missed-call list. Segment: hotel groups in Germany with a central office or call center.
2. **When (circumstance, occasion, window).** YC-L's "After hours. During peak hours. On holidays." *My choice:* the
   occasion "reservation shift", window the last 7 days (calls come in on every shift; spec 120's "every shift" -> 7
   DAYS), Frequency 5 to 7 days out of 7.
3. **Who pays (decision-maker `director`, Buyer and payer, Purchase friction).** TERMS addresses the hotel group;
   YC-L asks to "book a 10-minute call if you lead a hotel group". *My choice:* the revenue or reservations director
   decides, the hotel's owner has to agree. Purchase friction tests "A data protection review of guest calls" (German
   hotels handle guests' card and personal data on the call); my choice, no source names it.
4. **Mechanism.** YC-C: missed calls forwarded to Codyco, the AI answers, bookings appear in the PMS. Compatibility
   tests call forwarding (the mechanism needs it); Adoption friction tests letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice.
5. **Cost, price, ability.** As in the table. Reading `budget` by the engine (a percent of calls against euros).
6. **Commitment.** TERMS and YC-L: the paid, money-back pilot at one location. The step carries its number ("pay
   €3,000 for a money-back pilot at one hotel"), the gap-8 check.

## The respondents

No first-person account by a German reservation agent or revenue director was found in public (no HN thread; the
site's quotes are curated testimonials). **Every person is the author's invention**, no real person's name is used,
and each is built on the public facts named here.

Reservation agents (Parts 1 and 2):
- Lena Hoffmann: a trade-fair Saturday in a Munich central office; built on YC-L ("During peak hours") and the Munich
  hotel YC-L features.
- Murat Yilmaz: a check-in rush at the desk; YC-L's "peak hours".
- Chiara Russo: a group whose call center already answers after hours (YC-C: "Even with call centers..."); her pain is
  group emails, so Importance and Current solution go against the founder.
- Jonas Weber: alone on a Sunday desk; YC-L's "On holidays" / after hours.
- Aylin Demir: an old phone system that cannot forward (Compatibility only_with_help); the author's.
- Tobias Brandl: the sceptic who will not hand guests to an AI (Relative advantage negative, Adoption no); the author's.
- Elif Kaya: weekend abandoned calls seen on Monday; YC-L's "After hours".
- Daniel Okonkwo: rates pushed wrong to agencies matter more (Importance against); the author's.
- Mehmet Arslan: a vague story, GUESSED. Katarina Novak: a story chip, GUESSED.
- Florian Gruber, Nadia Haddad: gate No (no unanswered booking call in the 7 days).

Revenue directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3): Stefanie Wagner (6%), Andreas Keller (4%, below the founder's 5%),
Roberto Bianchi (8%), Ingrid Lindholm (2%, a call center covers after hours), Karim Benali (does not know his rate;
YC-L's "Free AI Strategy Workshop" and SITE's free test number as his ask), Petra Vogel (5%), Hannes Moser (nothing,
would not pay), Joanna Wiśniewska (10% at resort hotels in high season). The value boxes are percents of the calls, in
the founder's unit and period; the price picks are two codes, the pilot's rung and the licence's rung, each placed
against the founder's €3,000 and €1,000.

## Status today

Same idea (SITE, 2026-10-22): "Turn missed hotel calls into paid bookings.", widened to payments, invoices and
handovers; "Running at 15+ hotel groups" (the launch said 7); "€10k+ bookings written directly into the PMS". **No
public price today** (SITE and /faq show none); the €3,000 pilot terms remain the only priced source.

## Open (what could not be sourced, and the workarounds)

- **The licence amount** was never public. €1,000 to €1,500 per hotel a month is the operator's reading of the pilot's
  monthly rate (above). Treat the plan step's reading as a reading of that derivation.
- **Dollars or euros.** YC-L says "$5,000", YC-C "€5,000" for the same hotel; the pilot fee is in euros and the company
  is in Munich, so the entry is in euros. The market is DE, and the golden corpus's rule U (US only) is a note.
- **The "> 8 hotels" / "10 hotels" roll-out threshold** in TERMS and YC-L disagree; the entry does not use it.
- **Job titles.** Neither the agent nor the director is named in public; both are my choices (items 1 and 3).
- **The 5% is the founders' claim** for "the best" offices; no independent figure was sought.
- **UPFRONT_THEN has no "credited" or "money-back" flag**; the fee is a plain up-front amount (header).

screens.why7: My second row, setting which calls the AI hands to the desk, is a real step the agent takes; but the belief already on this screen, letting an AI answer in the hotel's voice, is closer to a permission the group's director grants than an effort the agent takes themselves, so the card's rule bends slightly.
screens.instead: What will reservation agents have to do to start using it? e.g. Set which calls the AI hands to the desk; Check the AI's bookings in the PMS each shift -- belief: Most would check the AI's bookings in the PMS each shift.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what they will have to do to start, Keel shows what it drafted from my answer for me to check, which is the obvious next step, though the intro repeats the title word for word.
screens.why2: Both rows are in a reservation agent's own words (the AI, the desk, guests, the hotel's voice) and read on first pass.
screens.why3: Whether they would let an AI take guests' calls and which calls they'd want handed back to the desk are things an agent in a central office or at the front desk knows from their own shift.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, both mine, under 9 words each, in the *their* voice, neither repeating call forwarding (Compatibility) or the data-protection review (Purchase friction).
screens.why5: Letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice is exactly the adoption friction I meant to test, and the belief keeps it word for word.
screens.why7: The second row is a step the agent takes themselves, but the tested first row is closer to accepting what the product does than to an effort they take on, and the habit first use really asks (picking up the AI's handovers and checking its bookings in the PMS) is not offered as Keel's suggested step.
screens.instead: What they'll have to do: Let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice · Set which calls the AI hands to the desk · (Keel's suggestion) Pick up the calls the AI hands back, with why: the new habit first use asks

screens.why1: Right after I checked the start-up efforts, picking which one I most fear will stop my reservation agents is the obvious next step before the test is built.
screens.why2: "Answer guests in the hotel's voice" and "hands to the desk" are how we talk in a reservations office, so I read both on the first pass.
screens.why3: Whether an agent would put up with an AI talking to their guests, and which calls they would want passed back, is something I hear from desk and central-office staff every week.
screens.why4: Two distinct efforts, one a change of habit and one a one-time setup, both in my words with nothing odd or overlapping, and nothing is missing for a pick of one.
screens.why5: The pick is my own adoption worry, letting the AI answer in the hotel's voice, kept word for word from what I typed.
screens.why7: Both rows are base-form, use the right voice and are under 9 words, the escape and balance work, and a sceptic like Tobias can refute it; but "let an AI answer guests" reads more as consenting to a change than as an effort the agent takes themselves, and whether the AI answers is partly the director's rollout call, so the measure is slightly bent.
screens.instead: Which one is most likely to stop them? -- Hand your missed booking calls to an AI that answers in the hotel's voice · Set which calls the AI hands back to the desk

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out is the obvious place to decide whether to collect pilot leads, and nothing earlier asked it.
screens.why2: "Offer a pilot?" with two plain options and a hint showing the exact line respondents will see is clear on first reading.
screens.why3: Whether I want pilot leads is my own call; I run pilots, so I can answer this straight away.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers the decision, the two options are distinct, and no escape is needed for a founder's own choice.
screens.why5: My pilot is a paid, money-back €3,000 pilot at one hotel that a director signs off, but the line "Would you try this for real? Leave your email" goes to reservation agents and reads like a free trial, so it drifts a little from what I offer.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would your hotel try this at one location? Leave your email and we'll put you in touch with whoever decides." (Yes, ask them / No pilot)

screens.why1: Choosing who interviews my reservation agents belongs right before the study goes out, after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but the hint mixes 'voice' with a video face and says Keel 'records the voice you pick once for this project', so I had to read it twice to see what the 400 credits buy.
screens.why3: I can judge which interviewer my agents in Germany would answer, so this is my call to make.
screens.why4: Two named voices with a 5-second sample are distinct, but nothing says whether either speaks German, and that is the one thing I need for agents in Munich or Berlin.
screens.why5: It keeps 'reservation agents' as I typed them and leaks nothing about Codyco to the respondent.
screens.instead: Who should ask reservation agents your questions, in German? Daphne (German, ▶ hear 5 s) / Saskia (German, ▶ hear 5 s). The face and voice you pick are recorded once for this project: 400 credits.

screens.why1: After choosing who asks the questions, deciding how the agents answer is the natural last setup step before sending.
screens.why2: Plain words throughout; 'read and tap', 'talking, typing or tapping' need no second read, and Daphne is explained as the AI interviewer.
screens.why3: I know my reservation agents work at a desk or headset between calls, so I can judge whether they would answer by video or by tapping.
screens.why4: Three distinct, complete options (Daphne, text, let them choose) with no overlap and nothing missing for this choice.
screens.why5: It names my respondents in my words, 'reservation agents', and my pick 'Read and tap' is shown as typed; nothing of Codyco leaks.

screens.why1: After choosing how reservation agents answer, deciding who receives the link is the obvious last step before sending.
screens.why2: The three choices are plain to a founder and say what each one does, including the Google sign-in on the open link.
screens.why3: I know whether I am reaching agents I know by name from our 7 hotel groups or posting in a hotel-trade group, so I can answer from my own situation.
screens.why4: Named people, a Keel contact search and one open group link are distinct, cover the realistic ways I would reach agents, and need no escape chip on a setup choice.
screens.why5: Nothing here alters my study or leaks Codyco's product or roles; it is only about distribution, and my pick of named people stands as I typed it.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right above '3 beliefs: 3 holding', and each card puts its count beside its bar, for example 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and why.
screens.why_b2: Each card says what was counted ('said yes, easily or most of the time', 'would do it'), over 7 people, and where the bar sits (5 of 7), all readable on first look.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry the belief lines I checked word for word, though Keel's solution statement above them is garbled ('the hotel's reservation agents the hotel forwards the call ... and gets back the confirmed booking').
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do next, such as the €3,000 money-back pilot as the step now that the solution holds, or that Relative advantage only just scraped by and three people on Adoption want a condition I should learn.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, but every card gets the same flat 'Holding up' and nothing says 7 is a small sample, even though Relative advantage sits exactly at the bar (5 of 7) and 3 of the 6 on Adoption agree only on a condition.
screens.instead: Holding up across 7 reservation agents, but only just: Relative advantage is exactly at the bar and half the Adoption yeses carry a condition, so read those conditions before pitching the €3,000 pilot; and write my solution as one clean sentence: missed calls forward to the AI, which answers in the hotel's voice and writes the booking into the PMS.

screens.why_b1: "Holding up" sits right beside "6 of 7 said yes, easily or most of the time · bar 5 of 7", so I see the verdict and the deciding number together.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts 5 easily, 1 most of the time, 1 only sometimes and 0 no, over 7 people, with the bar marked at 5 of 7, and I take it all in at a glance.
screens.why_b3: The title is Compatibility and the belief is word for word the one I checked: unanswered calls could be forwarded to another number.
screens.why_b4: The So line says forwarding won't stop hotel groups and sends me to Adoption friction, the belief I should worry about next.
screens.why_b5: It says the small group gives a lean, not a call. But the question shown is broken and asks a did-you act ("Did forward unanswer calls to another number?") against could-you answers like "most of the time", so I can't be sure the 6 of 7 means what the verdict claims.
screens.instead: Show the question as asked: "On your last reservation shift, could unanswered calls have been forwarded to another number?" Then add a line that some older phone systems need IT and the owner's money before forwarding works, as Aylin's quote shows.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside '5 of 7 said it would have gone better · bar 5 of 7 · at the bar', so I know it held and that it held only just.
screens.why_b2: The strip with its marker at 5 and '2 of 7 said no difference or worse' is plain, but 'Better · 5 5 a lot · 0 a little' with a doubled 5, plus 'Same' where the rule says 'no difference', needs a second look.
screens.why_b3: The title and the belief line are exactly what I checked, but the 'You said' line keeps only 'missed calls turned into bookings' and drops 'callers answered when the desk is busy', and the question asks about any time rather than the missed or busy call my advantage is for.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the 5 of 7 and points to Adoption friction, but it does not tell me that one more 'no difference' would sink this, or that Chiara's call-center group and Tobias's guests-want-a-person point to which hotel groups to target.
screens.why_b5: n of 7 is visible, it says 'at the bar', calls it 'a lean, not a call' and flags it as a hypothetical, so nothing is overclaimed.
screens.instead: Held exactly at the bar, 5 of 7 and all 5 'a lot', so one more 'no difference' flips it; the two against were a group whose call center already covers after hours and a desk that wants a person on the line, so test groups with no night cover next and check the busy-desk benefit too, not only missed calls.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and by what number.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the four answers over 7 people, and the strip shows 6 for, 1 against and the marker at 5, so all three read on first look.
screens.why_b3: The card's title is Adoption friction and its belief line is word for word the one I checked: let an AI answer guests in the hotel's voice.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me 3 hang on a condition and points below, but it does not say what the condition means for me: all three named the same one, never misquoting our rates or rules, and that is what my pilot has to prove.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the screen calls it a lean, not a call, and it splits the 6 into 3 as is and 3 on a condition, so it never calls this a strong yes.
screens.instead: Holding up, but only 3 of 7 would let it answer as is: the other 3 need it never to misquote your rates or rules, so make rate and policy accuracy the thing your pilot proves first.

screens.why_b1: Each box states the verdict, Holding up, with its deciding number beside it: 6 of 7 against a bar of 5 for Compatibility, and 5 of 7 at the bar for Relative advantage.
screens.why_b3: The dimension names and the belief lines are exactly the ones I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: The screen lays out the quotes but never says what they mean for me: that old phone systems need IT and the owner to pay, or that a group with an after-hours call center is the wrong first customer.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible, Relative advantage is marked at the bar rather than called strong, and each quote is labelled with that person's answer.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: phone systems that cannot forward without IT and an owner who will not pay, guests who ring wanting a person who knows the house, and group requests and emails as the real pain where a call center already covers after hours.
screens.instead: Under Relative advantage, say that I am exactly at the bar, so one more no would sink it, and that both noes come from groups already covered after hours or set on a human voice, so target groups without after-hours cover; also show the 3 conditional yeses on Adoption friction, since that is where the risk sits.

screens.why1: As the first screen it's the obvious screener: am I one of the people this study is about, and I sit in our central reservations office in Munich, so it fits.
screens.why2: Central reservations office and call center are what we call our own workplace, so I answer it at once.
screens.why3: Whether my hotel group runs a central reservations office is a plain fact of my job that I know without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes or No covers it completely for a gate, and the two don't overlap; no escape is right here.
screens.why5: It asks only about where I work, in the segment's own terms, and nothing about any product or plan reaches me.
screens.why6: One short question and two options; heard once, I'd just say yes.

screens.why1: Right after the screener about working in a central reservations office, it is natural to ask about my calls this past week before asking for a story.
screens.why2: Booking call and shift are my everyday words, and I can answer it at once.
screens.why3: I know exactly whether booking calls came in on my shifts this week; I take them all day.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for this question, and the two chips belong to the story box after a Yes, not to the gate.
screens.why5: The founder counted calls that do not get answered, at peak or after hours, but this asks only whether a call came in, which happens on every shift, so the founder's problem is gone.
screens.why6: Short, one question, then 'Yes or no', easy to hear once and answer.
screens.why7: The gate asks the circumstance instead of the problem, so every reservation agent at a Munich central office says Yes, No has nobody, and the founder's share can never be refuted, as in the card's bad example.
screens.instead: In the last 7 days, did a booking call to your office go unanswered on your shift? Yes · No

screens.why1: Right after confirming I took booking calls this week, showing me the idea before part 2 is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: PMS, OPERA Cloud, Sihot and Apaleo are everyday words at our desk, but "That is OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo" reads as if our PMS were all three, and "hands calls to your desk by your rules" leaves me guessing which rules.
screens.why3: Missed calls at peak, forwarding, taking payment and writing bookings into the PMS are exactly my Saturday on a trade-fair weekend.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is shown on purpose as an idea, in words my trade uses, and it still says an AI picks up the unanswered calls and books them through.
screens.why6: The how part runs five sentences, and the three system names after "That is" are a mouthful heard once, though nothing in it cannot be said.
screens.instead: Imagine Codyco, an AI reservation agent that answers the calls nobody picks up. Calls nobody answers go to it; it answers as your hotel, takes the payment, books straight into your PMS, such as OPERA Cloud, Sihot or Apaleo, and passes calls to your desk when you want. The people building it believe it would turn those calls into confirmed bookings.

screens.why1: Right after the Codyco card, asking whether my calls already roll over when nobody picks up is exactly what the idea leans on, so I see why it comes now.
screens.why2: "Did forward unanswer calls to another number?" has no subject and a broken word -- I have to guess whether it means did I forward them, did our phone system forward them, or could I have, and in the office we'd say "Rufumleitung" or "overflow" anyway.
screens.why3: Whether unanswered calls overflow is set by our telephony and IT, not something I do on a call, so on a busy trade-fair Saturday I'd half-know and half-guess how it was set up.
screens.why4: The could-you scale (easily, most of the time, only sometimes) does not answer a did-it question about a phone setting -- the true answer is just yes or no, so the middle rungs are odd for me.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product leaks past the card, but the clause is clipped and garbled ("Did forward unanswer"), so the founder's condition reaches me drifted, not kept.
screens.why6: Heard aloud, "Did forward unanswer calls to another number?" is not a sentence a listener can parse once -- no subject, a missing "-ed" -- and "your last call" is vague about which call.
screens.why7: The condition is a fact about the phone setup (a forwarding rule exists) yet it is served the ability four, which the card forbids for a fact (it must be Yes · Yes, with some steps · No), and asked as a did-you act so the graded options have no true answer; it also tests forwarding, not whether the idea can take the unanswered calls.
screens.instead: Think of your last busy shift. Could the calls nobody picked up have been sent on to another number? Yes · Yes, with some steps · No · or I can't tell.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card, asking whether Codyco would have done my calls better is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: "The most recent time you had to turn every guest who calls into a booking" is not how I talk about a shift; I had to read it twice to see it means my last busy shift on the phones.
screens.why3: I know my shifts, but turning every caller into a booking isn't one moment I can point to, so I would be guessing which time it means.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference and worse cover it cleanly, and "I can't tell" fits as the way out.
screens.why5: The founder's own job line was dropped into my question word for word, so it reads like their pitch rather than my day.
screens.why6: The four options and the escape say well, but the long "turn every guest who calls into a booking" clause is a mouthful to hear once.
screens.why7: The measure, the four fixed answers, the balance and the escape are all right, but the occasion is not the hard case the advantage is for, such as the last peak-hour rush when calls went unanswered, and the stem drops what Codyco is.
screens.instead: Think of your last busy shift when calls came in faster than you could pick up. Would Codyco, an AI agent that answers the calls nobody picks up, have handled that better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea card and whether it would do better, asking whether I'd actually take it on is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: "In your hotel's voice" made me read twice: does it mean a real voice that sounds like our desk, or our brand's tone? Neither is how we'd say it at the office.
screens.why3: Whether an AI answers our guests is something the group's management decides, not me on a trade-fair Saturday, so I'd be half guessing about my bosses.
screens.why4: Yes, a real condition, probably not and no are distinct, and the misquoting-rates catch is exactly what I'd worry about; I can't tell fits.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks beyond the idea card shown on purpose, and the step still reads as letting the AI pick up the calls we miss.
screens.why6: Short, one question, four options I can hold, one escape at the end, and the spoken "your rates" sounds right aloud.
screens.why7: The options and escape are the card's shape and the condition is mine, but letting it answer guests is more a permission the hotel gives than an effort I take myself to start using it, so the measure is bent.
screens.instead: To use Codyco, you'd look over the calls it took at the start of each shift. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Only if it didn't hold up my live calls · Probably not · No · I can't tell
